question: to the Commission Fredis Beleris (PPE) Subject:

In the village of Zvërnec, Vlora Region, which is primarily inhabited by members of the Greek ethnic minority, it is alleged that a private company is intervening and encroaching on land and properties that were illegally seized by the communist regime in the 1960s and have not yet been returned to their rightful owners. At the same time, during peaceful protests by residents about the injustice they have suffered, incidents of violence and intimidation by individuals allegedly associated with the company were recorded, even in the presence of police forces. These incidents raise serious questions regarding respect for fundamental freedoms, property rights and the protection of recognised national minorities in a country that is a candidate for accession to the European Union. In view of this: 1.

Is the Commission aware of the allegations of violence and intimidation against residents of Zvërnec during peaceful protests and does it intend to seek clarification from the Albanian authorities on the safeguarding of the right to protest?
What measures is the Commission taking to protect the fundamental rights of recognised ethnic minorities, including their property rights, in the candidate countries?

Given that the Commission is in contact with the Albanian competent authorities, how does it ensure the objectivity of the findings of the Interim Benchmark Assessment Report (IBAR) and annual reports of the Commission?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (18.8.2026) The Commission is closely following developments in Albania and it is aware of the protests referred to by Honourable Member. The Commission also notes that the protests have been largely peaceful. Freedom of assembly and expression are fundamental rights and core European values and should be respected. The Commission monitors closely fulfilment of such fundamentals rights and values, and it is in continuous contact with the Albanian authorities and civil society. In the context of the accession process, the Commission monitors and reports also on property rights and on the rights of persons belonging to minorities in its annual report on Albania. The annual report 2026 is currently being drafted and will reflect the Commission’s assessment of Albania’s progress in these areas since 2025. All documents drafted by the Commission, including the Interim Benchmark Assessment Report, the Interim EU Common Position and the annual reports, follow a precise methodology which requires the very regular consultation of a wide variety of interlocutors other than the Albanian authorities. The insights of international organisations, civil society organisations, independent agencies, monitoring bodies and experts are taken in due consideration when making assessments of Albania’s progress.
